title: 131. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Comparing Relative Measurement Uncertainties
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct expression for relative uncertainty.
questions.question: Which expression correctly gives the relative uncertainty of a measurement?
questions.explanation: Relative uncertainty compares the absolute error bound with the positive measured value by division. Multiplying them instead gives units of the measurement squared and is not a relative quantity.
questions.hint: A relative quantity should be dimensionless.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage relative uncertainty of a length measurement.
questions.question: A length is measured as \((5.0 \pm 0.1)\text{ cm}\). What is its relative uncertainty as a percentage?
questions.explanation: The relative fraction is \(\frac{0.1}{5.0}=0.02\), or \(2\%\). The alternative \(0.2\%\) moves the decimal point only one place instead of two when reporting a percentage.
questions.hint: Distinguish the size of an error from its size relative to the measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which of two measurements has the smaller relative uncertainty.
questions.question: Which measurement has the smaller relative uncertainty?
questions.explanation: The first relative fraction is \(\frac{0.1}{10.0}=0.01=1\%\); the second is \(\frac{0.1}{2.0}=0.05=5\%\). The first is smaller. Equal absolute bounds do not imply equal relative bounds; the smaller length has the larger relative error.
questions.hint: Compare each absolute error with the size of its own measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which mass measurement has the smaller relative uncertainty.
questions.question: Which measurement has the smaller relative uncertainty?
questions.explanation: The relative fractions are \(\frac{1}{20}=0.05=5\%\) and \(\frac{2}{50}=0.04=4\%\). The second is smaller. The alternative compares only the absolute bounds and ignores the different measured masses.
questions.hint: Compare an absolute error with the size of its own measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage relative uncertainty of a measurement in metres.
questions.question: A distance is \((8.0 \pm 0.2)\text{ m}\). What is the relative uncertainty as a percentage?
questions.explanation: The relative fraction is \(\frac{0.2}{8.0}=0.025\), or \(2.5\%\). The alternative \(0.25\%\) moves the decimal point only one place instead of two.
questions.hint: Distinguish the size of an error from its size relative to the measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the absolute uncertainty from a given relative uncertainty.
questions.question: A measurement has value \(50\text{ cm}\) and relative uncertainty \(4\%\). What is its absolute uncertainty?
questions.explanation: The absolute bound is \(50\times 0.04=2\text{ cm}\). The alternative \(0.2\text{ cm}\) uses \(0.4\%\) of the measurement rather than \(4\%\).
questions.hint: Write the percentage as a decimal fraction and apply it to the measured value.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which measurement is relatively more precise.
questions.question: Two lengths are \((1.00 \pm 0.05)\text{ m}\) and \((5.00 \pm 0.10)\text{ m}\). Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The second measurement has the smaller relative uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: The first measurement has the smaller relative uncertainty.

questions.explanation: The relative fractions are \(\frac{0.05}{1.00}=0.05=5\%\) and \(\frac{0.10}{5.00}=0.02=2\%\). The second is smaller. The alternative compares only the absolute bounds, even though their measured values also differ.
questions.hint: Compare an absolute error with the size of its own measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether two measurements have equal relative uncertainties.
questions.question: Compare \((12.0 \pm 0.3)\text{ cm}\) and \((4.0 \pm 0.1)\text{ cm}\). Which conclusion is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The first measurement has a larger relative uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: The two measurements have equal relative uncertainties.

questions.explanation: The relative fractions are \(\frac{0.3}{12.0}=0.025\) and \(\frac{0.1}{4.0}=0.025\). They are equal. The alternative ignores that the first measurement and its bound are both three times the second.
questions.hint: Distinguish the size of an error from its size relative to the measurement.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate the percentage relative uncertainty of a measured length.
questions.question: A length is \((2.50 \pm 0.02)\text{ m}\). What is the relative uncertainty as a percentage?
questions.explanation: The relative fraction is \(\frac{0.02}{2.50}=0.008\), or \(0.8\%\). The alternative \(0.08\%\) moves the decimal point only one place instead of two.
questions.hint: Convert a dimensionless fraction to a percentage only when requested.

questions.concept: Comparing Relative Uncertainties in a Derived Quantity
questions.learningObjective: Determine which measurement contributes the larger relative uncertainty to a calculated density.
questions.question: A mass is \((50.0 \pm 0.5)\text{ g}\) and a volume is \((20.0 \pm 0.4)\text{ cm}^3\). The density is calculated as \(\frac{m}{V}\). Which measurement contributes the larger relative uncertainty to the density?

options.label: A
options.text: The volume measurement contributes the larger relative uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: The mass measurement contributes the larger relative uncertainty.

questions.explanation: The mass contributes relative bound \(\frac{0.5}{50.0}=0.01=1\%\); the volume contributes \(\frac{0.4}{20.0}=0.02=2\%\). The volume contribution is larger. Comparing only the absolute numbers would incorrectly favour the mass.
questions.hint: Compare an absolute error with the size of its own measurement.
